slides.title: Introduction to ROS2
slides.text:
Introduction to ROS2

•  ROS2 stands for Robot Operating System 2.
•  Open-source middleware for robotics.
•  Provides communication framework for robots.
•  Supports distributed systems.
•  Real-time communication support.
•  Data Distribution System (DDS) - based communication
   architecture.
•  Multi-robot communication.
•  Widely used in research and industry.





                                                                                                           3

visualInspection.notes: Text-only introduction: Robot Operating System2 name, open-source middleware, distributed communication, real-time support, DDS-based architecture and multi-robot communication. Footer3. Support is not a demonstrated hard timing guarantee; do not call this an OS kernel.

slides.title: Why ROS2 for Autonomous Navigation?
slides.text:
Why ROS2 for Autonomous Navigation?

•  Modular architecture.
•  Large robotics ecosystem.
•  Sensor integration support.
•  Real-time navigation capabilities.
•  Strong simulation support.
•  Supports AI and machine learning integration.
•  Applications
   –  Autonomous mobile robots
   –  Warehouse robots
   –  Service robots
   –  Delivery robots

                                                                                                           4

visualInspection.notes: Text-only motivations: modularity, sensor integration, ecosystem, real-time capabilities, simulation and AI/ML integration; mobile/warehouse/service/delivery applications. Footer4. Middleware capabilities do not by themselves implement a safe navigation policy.

slides.title: Introduction to Gazebo Simulator
slides.text:
Introduction to Gazebo Simulator
•  3D robotics simulator.
•  Simulates sensors and physics.
•  Provides realistic robot environments.
•  Supports multiple robot platforms.
•  Integrates with ROS and ROS2.
•  Core Components
   –  Physics Engine
   –  Rendering Engine
   –  Sensor Engine
   –  User Interface
   –  Transport Layer (handles communication between
        distributed nodes)

                                                                                                           5

visualInspection.notes: Actual Gazebo Classic-style window with empty grid scene, left world panel, bottom simulation controls; screenshot is illustrative, not executed. Text distinguishes physics/rendering/sensor engines, UI and transport, 3D simulation and ROS integration. Footer5. Realistic simulation is not identical-to-hardware proof.

slides.title: Gazebo Building Editor
slides.text:
Gazebo Building Editor

•  Tool for creating indoor environments.
•  Used to design walls, rooms, obstacles.
•  Helpful for navigation experiments.
•  Creates simulation worlds quickly.
•  Steps to Create a Simulation World
     1.  Open Building Editor
     2.  Draw walls and rooms
     3.  Add doors and windows
     4.  Assign textures
     5.  Save building model
     6.  Export to Gazebo world

                                                                                                           6

visualInspection.notes: Actual Building Editor screenshot has palette at left (walls/windows/doors/stairs/colors/textures), 2D plan above, 3D view below. Six-step construction list: open, walls/rooms, doors/windows, textures, save building, export world. Footer6. Scope is pictured Gazebo Classic editor, not all newer Gazebo interfaces.

slides.title: Gazebo Model Editor
slides.text:
Gazebo Model Editor

•  Used to create custom robot
   models.
•  Supports links and joints.
•  Allows sensor integration.
•  Generates Simulation Description
   Format (SDF) models.
•  Capabilities
   – Add geometric shapes
   –  Configure inertial properties
   –  Define collision elements
   –  Attach plugins


                                                                                                           7

visualInspection.notes: Model Editor screenshot shows cylinder, sphere and box shapes and model database. Text: custom robots, links/joints, sensors, SDF, inertial properties, collision elements and plugins. Footer7. Visible geometry, collision and inertial definitions have distinct roles.

slides.title: ROS Visualization Tool (RViz)
slides.text:
ROS Visualization Tool (RViz)

 •  RViz provides a graphical interface to:
    –  Visualize robot models
    –  Display sensor data
    –  Monitor robot localization
    –  View SLAM-generated maps
    –  Analyze navigation paths
    –  Debug robot behavior
    –  Send navigation goals
 •  Gazebo simulates the robot and environment, while
    RViz visualizes and monitors the robot's state, sensors,
    maps, and navigation data.


                                                                                                           8

visualInspection.notes: RViz screenshot toolbar includes 2D Pose Estimate and 2D Goal Pose; display tree/fixed-frame settings left, views right, central grid and time/status below. Text lists models/sensors/localization/maps/paths/debugging/goals and explicitly distinguishes Gazebo simulation from visualization. Footer8. UI goal label can vary with plugin/configuration; later slides show Nav2 Goal.

slides.title: Robot Description Formats: URDF and SDF
slides.text:
Robot Description Formats: URDF and SDF
•  URDF
   –  Unified Robot Description Format
   –  eXtensible Markup Language(XML)-based description
   – Commonly used in ROS2
•  SDF
   –  Simulation Description Format
   – More detailed simulation support
   –  Used heavily in Gazebo
•  Difference
   –  URDF: Robot structure
   –  SDF: Full simulation environment


                                                                                                             9

visualInspection.notes: URDF/XML robot description versus SDF fuller simulation support. Right figure labels robot alone URDF and robot/building/tree world SDF. Footer9. This is a scope emphasis, not proof SDF cannot describe an individual robot; preceding1849 explicitly calls generated outputs SDF models.

slides.title: Gazebo Plugins
slides.text:
Gazebo Plugins

•  A plugin is a chunk of code (in C/C++) that is compiled as
   a shared library and inserted into the simulation.
•  Gazebo  plugins  give  your  URDF  models  greater
   functionality and can tie in ROS messages and service
    calls for sensor output and motor input.
•  World Plugins: Affect simulation world
•  Model Plugins: Control robot models
•  Sensor Plugins: Sensor-specific functionality
•  GUI Plugins: Extend graphical interface





                                                                                                          10

visualInspection.notes: Text-only Classic-style plugin description: C/C++ shared library inserted into simulation; links ROS messages/service calls to sensor output and motor input. Four scopes world/model/sensor/GUI. Footer10. No source code, compilation command or plugin binary supplied.

slides.title: SLAM Basics
slides.text:
SLAM Basics

•  Simultaneous Localization and Mapping.
•  A technique used by robots to:
   –  Build a map
   –  Estimate robot position simultaneously
•  Importance
   – Unknown environment exploration
   –  Autonomous navigation
   –  Real-time localization





                                                                                                          11

visualInspection.notes: Text-only SLAM definition simultaneously estimates robot position and builds map; exploration/navigation/localization roles. Footer11. Distinguish building unknown map from localizing in an existing map; no estimator formula printed.

slides.title: SLAM Workflow
slides.text:
SLAM Workflow

SLAM Process
     1.  Sensor data acquisition
     2.  Feature extraction
     3.  Pose estimation
     4.  Map update
     5.  Loop closure (correct accumulated error)
Output
   –  Occupancy grid map
   –  Robot trajectory





                                                                                                          12

visualInspection.notes: Left five-stage acquisition/features/pose/map/loop-closure list. Right actual diagram: sensor-dependent front end(feature extraction,data association,feature tracking,loop closure)→sensor-independent back end(MAP estimation, graph optimization:pose graph,factor graph)→estimated trajectory/map; curved arrow feeds back from back end to front end. Footer12. Loop closure detection versus correction/optimization distinct; MAP is estimator acronym in diagram, not just occupancy-map label.

slides.title: Occupancy Grid Mapping
slides.text:
Occupancy Grid Mapping

•  An  occupancy  grid map   is  a  foundational  spatial
   representation  used  in  robotics  and  autonomous
   navigation to map environments.
•  Map Representation.
•   Cell States
   –  Occupied
   –  Free
   –  Unknown
•  Advantages
   –  Easy implementation
   –  Suitable for navigation
   –  Efficient path planning

                                                                                                          13

visualInspection.notes: Actual figure: yellow robot cell, red wedge outlines field of view, white free cells, black occupied strip and grey unknown cells. Explicit label arrows identify each. Footer13. Unknown is not observed free; map representation is not geometric certainty or all-white collision safety.

slides.title: SLAM Demonstration Workflow in ROS2
slides.text:
SLAM Demonstration Workflow in ROS2

Mapping Process
    1)  Launch Gazebo world
    2) Spawn robot model
    3)  Launch SLAM toolbox
    4)  Teleoperate robot
    5)  Generate occupancy map
    6)  Save generated map
Generated Files
   –  map.yaml (configuration file that stores metadata
       about a saved map)
   – map.pgm (Portable Gray Map in grayscale)

                                                                                                          14

visualInspection.notes: Text-only sequence world→spawn→SLAM toolbox→teleoperate→occupancy map→save. Files map.yaml metadata and map.pgm grayscale. Footer14. Later1868 actually launches Cartographer, not SLAM Toolbox; preserve these as alternative source workflows rather than claim same package.

slides.title: ROS Navigation Stack (NAV)
slides.text:
ROS Navigation Stack (NAV)
•  Enables mobile robots to autonomously move from point
  A to point B.
Main Components
   –  move_base
   –  global_planner
   –  local_planner
   –  costmap_2d (for navigation, using sensor data and/or a
          static map to represent obstacles and traversable space)
   –  Amcl (Adaptive Monte Carlo Localization)
Features
   – Path planning
   – Obstacle avoidance
   –  Localization

                                                                                                          15

visualInspection.notes: Legacy ROS Navigation Stack component names move_base,global_planner,local_planner,costmap_2d,AMCL; path planning, obstacle avoidance and localization roles. Footer15. Distinguish this NAV list from ROS2 NAV2 servers on1859.

slides.title: NAV Architecture
slides.text:
NAV Architecture

 Input
    – Map
    –  Sensor data
    –  Odometry
 Processing
    –  Localization
    –  Global planning
    –  Local planning
    –  Recovery behaviors
 Output
    –  Velocity commands

                                                                                                          16

visualInspection.notes: Detailed original NAV diagram: goal move_base_simple/goal geometry_msgs/PoseStamped→global_planner; global→local internal nav_msgs/Path; odom nav_msgs/Odometry→local; local→base controller cmd_vel geometry_msgs/Twist. Sensor LaserScan/PointCloud topics feed both costmaps; map_server /map GetMap to global_costmap; tf/tfMessage links localization/sensor transforms/odometry. Legend provided/optional/platform-specific nodes. Footer16. This is legacy ROS1 naming; do not relabel message types as ROS2. Both costmaps receive sensor arrows, constraining later static/global shorthand.

slides.title: Introduction to ROS2 Navigation Stack (NAV2)  The Behavior
slides.text:
Introduction to ROS2 Navigation Stack (NAV2)  The Behavior
                                                           Server is the
Core NAV2                                                  component that
Components                                                          handles behaviors
•  Planner Server                                                        such as recovery
•  Controller Server                                          actions and docking.
•  Behaviour Tree (BT)
   Navigator
•  Recovery Server
•  Map Server
•  Adaptive Monte
   Carlo Localization
   (AMCL)


                                                                                                            17

visualInspection.notes: Actual NAV2 architecture diagram: BT Navigator Server top, lifecycle manager, controller(local costmap), planner(global costmap), behavior, smoother(costmap/footprint subscription), route server; dashed waypoint follower/autonomy above; controller→velocity smoother→collision monitor→robot base below. Sensor arrows to local and global costmaps; BT/TF/map inputs. Text list says Recovery Server but drawing says Behavior Server. Right prose attributes recovery and docking to Behavior Server. Footer17. Need primary version qualification: diagram/current components cannot all be assumed present in Humble demo; dedicated docking architecture must be checked before treating prose universally.

slides.title: Global Planner in NAV2
slides.text:
Global Planner in NAV2

 •  For path planning
 •  Purpose
    –  Compute collision-free path
 •  Popular Global Planners
    –  NavFn Planner (Dijkstra/A*)
    –  Smac Planner
    –  Theta Star Planner
 •  Inputs
    –  Occupancy map
    –  Goal position



                                                                                                          19

visualInspection.notes: Text-only global planning: collision-free path, NavFn(Dijkstra/A*),Smac,Theta Star; inputs list occupancy map and goal. Footer19. This abbreviated list omits explicit start pose/robot footprint/feasibility; path safety is relative to model/map, not a universal physical guarantee.

slides.title: Local Planner / Controller
slides.text:
Local Planner / Controller

 •  For motion control
 •  Purpose
    –  Follow global path safely
    –  Generate velocity commands
 •  Popular Local Planners
    –  Dynamic Window Approach (DWA)
    –  Timed Elastic Band (TEB)
 •  Inputs
    –  Global path
    –  Sensor data
    –  Robot state

                                                                                                          20

visualInspection.notes: Text-only local planner/controller: follow global path safely, generate velocity commands; DWA and TEB named; inputs global path,sensor data,robot state. Footer20. Treat named algorithms as source examples, not proof of installed Nav2 Humble plugin names or defaults.

slides.title: Costmaps in NAV2
slides.text:
Costmaps in NAV2

 Navigation Costmaps
 •  Global Costmap
    –  Static map representation
 •   Local Costmap
    –  Dynamic obstacle updates
 •  Layers
    –  Static layer
    –  Obstacle layer
    –  Inflation layer





                                                                                                          21

visualInspection.notes: Text-only costmaps: global described as static map representation; local as dynamic obstacle updates; layers static, obstacle and inflation. Footer21. This is a simplification, not an exclusivity rule: sensor arrows actually feed both global and local costmaps on1858/1859, so global may include changing obstacles.

slides.title: Localization using Adaptive Monte Carlo Localization (AMCL)
slides.text:
Localization using Adaptive Monte Carlo Localization (AMCL)

 Adaptive Monte Carlo Localization
 •  Purpose
    –  Estimate robot pose
 •  Inputs
    –  LiDAR scan
    –  Occupancy map
    –  Odometry
 •  Method
    –  Particle filter localization





                                                                                                          22

visualInspection.notes: Text-only AMCL: estimates robot pose from LiDAR scan, occupancy map and odometry using particle-filter localization. Footer22. Known-map localization differs from constructing an unknown map. No weight equations printed; any particle arithmetic must supply its own weights and assumptions.

slides.title: NAV2 in ROS2
slides.text:
NAV2 in ROS2

Install the Nav2 packages
    $ sudo apt install ros-humble-navigation2
    ros-humble-nav2-bringup
   –  Install the packages for the robot
        (Turtlebot3).
    $ sudo apt install ros-humble-turtlebot3*
   – Add this line at the end of your .bashrc:
       export TURTLEBOT3_MODEL=waffle.
   –  Start the simulated robot in a Gazebo world.
    $ ros2 launch turtlebot3_gazebo
    turtlebot3_world.launch.py


                                                                                                          25

visualInspection.notes: Actual commands: sudo apt install ros-humble-navigation2 [visual wrap] ros-humble-nav2-bringup; sudo apt install ros-humble-turtlebot3*; export TURTLEBOT3_MODEL=waffle. with a literal black period immediately after red waffle; ros2 launch turtlebot3_gazebo turtlebot3_world.launch.py. Gazette screenshot shows robot scan rays/obstacles, not evidence any command was executed here. Footer25. Literal period changes environment value; intended model requires explicit repair. Package command first line wraps without shell continuation; transcribe as displayed and separately normalized single command.
